title: The substituted Class and the two-stage analysis
paras: Right — Class Q. This is the one that lets you turn an agricultural building into housing without ever having to argue the planning merits of a home in the countryside. That's why everyone wants it, and it's exactly why it's the most fought-over permitted development right there is. More appeals, more refusals, more technical argument than anything else round here. And it rewards preparation like nothing else, because whether you qualify comes down to the history and the fabric of the building — and you have to prove all of it, not just assert it.

The one thing to know before you touch a Class Q case today: the whole right was rewritten in 2024. Not amended — replaced, wholesale. New eligibility, new numbers, a whole new category of building let in. The old version has had its transitional period and it's gone now, so every fresh application runs on the new Class. What that means in practice is you treat anything you remember from the old days — and a lot of the older appeal decisions — with real caution. The precise references, the dates and the paragraph numbers are all in the written guide; I'll stay out of the citations here and keep us on the ideas.

The single most useful thing to carry through the whole topic is this. Class Q is a two-stage test, and blurring the two is the commonest mistake on either side of the desk. Stage one is eligibility — is this even within the Class at all? That's hard-edged: facts about the building, its history, the size caps, the works you're allowed. No discretion, and fail any one of them and you're out. Stage two only matters if you're through stage one, and it asks something completely different — is it acceptable on a short, closed list of things like flooding, highways and noise? That's judgement.

And two things sit over all of it. The development plan barely gets a look in — not at stage one, and only in a narrow way at stage two. And the burden is entirely on you. There's no benefit of the doubt: leave something unproven and it counts against you. On top of that, the whole scheme has to fit within the Class. One element outside it, and nothing's permitted — you don't get the compliant bits for free.

title: Qualifying buildings: the two gateways
paras: So — which buildings actually qualify? Since the 2024 rewrite there are two different routes in, and the very first thing you do on any instruction is work out which route you're on, because the tests aren't the same. The first route is the straightforward one: a building that's part of a working farm. And what changed in 2024 is what you no longer have to show. It doesn't have to have been used only for agriculture, and it doesn't even have to be in agricultural use when you apply. What matters is that it was genuinely part of the farm holding at the relevant cut-off date. So that old fight about sole agricultural use has largely gone — a barn on a farm that also happens to have a few non-farm bits stored in it isn't knocked out on that alone any more.

The second route is the big new one, and it's where you earn your fee — the former agricultural building. One that used to be part of a farm but isn't any more. There's a condition here that is absolutely unforgiving, so hold onto it: once that building left the farm, it must never have been used for anything non-agricultural. Not briefly, not minor, not oh, someone parked a van in it for a while. Any non-farm use after it left the holding, and it's dead — permanently, and nothing brings it back. That single point ends more of these cases than everything else put together. There are also timing conditions — how long since it left the farm — and the exact periods are, again, in the written guide.

A word on what agricultural actually means, because it has teeth. We're talking agriculture as a trade or business — so hobby farming, a few amenity horses, the domestic paddock, none of that counts, however green and rural it looks. Equestrian use isn't agriculture, apart from simple grazing. Livery, kennels, rural storage businesses — not agriculture. And crucially, none of this history is presumed. You prove it. Dated photographs, farm accounts and invoices, tenancy papers, holding numbers, and honest, specific statutory declarations from people who actually know. Inspectors weigh those declarations against the hard evidence and quietly discount the vague and the self-interested. If the lawful use is genuinely arguable, sort it out with a certificate of lawfulness before you ever get to the prior approval application.

Then there are a few traps sitting in the background that get missed at appraisal, and any one of them is fatal. If there's an agricultural tenancy, you need both the landlord and the tenant to consent. If a tenancy was ended in the year before the development, for the purpose of the development, you're blocked unless there's written agreement the land's no longer needed for farming. And here's the sting for the diversifying farm: if a new agricultural building has gone up on the unit under the Part 6 farming rights in the last ten years, Class Q is shut off for that whole unit. So the grain store the farmer put up a few years back can quietly kill the barn conversion next door. Last thing — the building has to be structurally capable of becoming a house using only the limited works you're allowed. That's a job for a chartered engineer, speaking to capability, and its absence is a classic reason these get refused.

title: The unit, the original limits and the caps
paras: Now, the unit and the caps — and this is where a lot of thin cases quietly die. The agricultural unit is about occupation, not ownership: what land is actually farmed together as one holding? You work it out the same way you'd work out a planning unit. Title boundaries and tenancy documents are evidence, but none of them settles it. Land in different ownership farmed as one holding can be a single unit; neighbouring fields in the same ownership farmed separately can be several. And if you assert the unit rather than prove it, an inspector is perfectly entitled to dismiss the appeal on that alone.

There are three size limits, and they all bite at once. No single dwelling bigger than 150 square metres. No more than ten dwellings. And no more than a thousand square metres in total — and that total counts everything ever done under Class Q on that unit, including the old versions of the right. So the headroom is whatever's left after the history. A unit that's already produced, say, five dwellings and seven hundred square metres has five dwellings and three hundred square metres left, and that's it.

The reason it's drawn that way is anti-avoidance, and it has sharp commercial edges. You can't chop a holding up, sell it in bits, or reorganise it to conjure fresh allowances — the caps attach to the historic footprint of the whole original unit. Which means if you buy part of a farm, you inherit the Class Q history of all of it. So on any rural land deal, finding out what's already been converted under Class Q across that original unit is a proper piece of due diligence — an undocumented history isn't a technicality, it's a priced risk. And if you're only converting part of a big building to stay within the caps, the drawings have to define exactly which part, because that line fixes both the floorspace sum and where the residential planning unit ends up. Be vague here and you're banking a future argument about what was actually approved.

title: Building operations, Hibbitt and the conversion boundary
paras: Let's talk about how much building work you're actually allowed to do — because this is where a lot of Class Q schemes fall apart. The right lets you convert the building, and it gives you a short, closed list of works to do it with: new windows, doors, a roof, external walls, the services — water, drainage, electricity — and just enough partial demolition to carry those out. That's it. If a job isn't on that list, it doesn't matter how sensible it is, it's outside the Class. And even the works that are on the list have to go no further than the conversion genuinely needs. The key line the guidance draws is this: you can't build new structural elements. If the building can't take the conversion without a new frame, new load-bearing walls, or effectively rebuilding it, then what you're doing isn't a conversion at all.

And that's really the whole battleground, so let me give you the case it all turns on — Hibbitt. Picture a steel-framed farm building, largely open on three sides, barely any cladding. The owner wanted to turn it into a house; it was refused, and the court backed the refusal. The principle that came out of it is the one to carry with you: Class Q permits a conversion, but not works so major that, in practical reality, what you're really doing is a rebuild, or a new build from scratch. And here's the subtle part — it's judged as a whole. Even if you can point at each individual operation and say, well, that one's on the list, if the totality of what you're doing amounts to reconstruction, the whole scheme falls outside the Class. The starting point has to be a building that's genuinely capable of being converted in the first place.

So, practically? Open-sided, skeletal, half-derelict barns are poor candidates, and no amount of clever drafting fixes that. And don't be tempted to understate the works to sneak through prior approval — because anything you build beyond what's permitted is simply unlawful, whatever the approval letter says. This is exactly why the structural engineer's report earns its money. It has to speak to capability, not just condition — can this building actually be converted using only the permitted works? If the honest answer involves underpinning, new foundations, or replacing the frame, that's your signal to stop and go for a full planning application instead. Trying to force it through Class Q just buys you an enforcement problem down the line.

One more practical control worth knowing. As a rule you can't push the building's outer dimensions beyond what's already there — the envelope is fixed. There are just two exceptions. There's the small single-storey rear extension the 2024 changes brought in, and it's tightly drawn: rear only, one storey, a few metres at most, no higher than the existing eaves, and only over ground that's already hard-surfaced. And there's a small tolerance — a couple of hundred millimetres — to let you add things like external insulation or cladding without technically breaching the envelope. That's a tolerance for making the conversion work, not a licence for design ambition. And you can't lean on that extension to hit the space standard — the standard is judged on the existing building without it.

title: Prior approval: the matters
paras: Right — you're through eligibility, so now stage two: prior approval. This is a closed list of things the council can consider, and nothing else. For the usual case — a change of use with building works — there are seven of them: highways and transport, noise, contamination, flooding, then a Class Q special called location and siting, the design and external appearance of the building, and adequate natural light to the habitable rooms. If there are no building works it's six, because design drops away. And if you've got the little extension, you add its impact on the neighbours. The thing to hold onto is that a refusal on any single one of these defeats the whole application — and eligibility still comes first, so expect the council to test whether you're really in the Class before it even gets to these.

Let me flag the ones that actually cause trouble. Highways first — and there's a trap here. The prior approval matter is about the impact of the traffic: is the access safe, can the lane cope, what about refuse and deliveries. But sitting separately, back in eligibility, is an absolute requirement that the building already has suitable access to a public highway. Those are two different things, and the classic mistake is trying to fix an eligibility access problem by offering to build a new access. You can't. If suitable access doesn't already exist, no amount of engineering works cures it.

Noise cuts both ways on a farm — you're protecting your future residents from grain driers, livestock and machinery, and a scheme that jams houses up against a working yard gets refused, if not on noise then on location and siting. Which is the big one, and it's unique to Class Q. It asks whether the location or siting makes it impractical or undesirable for the building to become a home — impractical meaning not sensible or realistic, undesirable meaning genuinely harmful or objectionable. It is emphatically not a way to run development plan policy, or a general sustainability test, through the back door — a barn can pass here in a spot where a planning application for a new house would be refused flat. The buildings that genuinely fail are the ones in the working heart of a farmyard, or ringed by intensive livestock, or somewhere physically hazardous or impossible to reach. Just being isolated, on its own, is a weak reason to refuse.

And keep an eye on natural light, because it quietly kills deep-plan barns. The council has to be satisfied every habitable room gets adequate light, and they'll want floor plans with the window positions and dimensions actually on them — vague plans, or a bedroom lit by one doubtful rooflight, and you're refused. Contamination and flooding round out the list: on a farm, think fuel stores, sheep dip, old pesticides and asbestos roofs for contamination; and for flooding it's about keeping the residents safe — a proper flood risk assessment in the higher-risk areas, not a debate about whether there's a better site down the road.

title: Procedure, the 56 days and the space standard
paras: Now the procedure, and it's genuinely important because the timing has teeth. You put in your application — a description that actually states the works you're relying on, a site plan, floor plans that deal with natural light, and the fee. The council can refuse if it thinks you're not in the Class, or if you simply haven't given it enough to judge compliance — that's legitimate, though some authorities misuse it to demand material the rules don't require. They'll notify the neighbours and consult the highway authority, and the Environment Agency where there's flooding.

Here's the part to diarise. You can't start until you've got the decision in writing, or fifty-six days have passed — whichever comes first. And if they simply say nothing for fifty-six days, you've got deemed consent: you can proceed in line with what you submitted. That period can be extended, but only by written agreement — an email exchange is enough. Treat any request for more time as a real strategic decision, not a courtesy: agree, and you've handed back your deemed consent; refuse, and you'll usually just get a refusal on the papers. Either way, count the fifty-six days from receipt and put day fifty-six in the diary.

One caution on deemed consent, though — it only ever protects a development that's genuinely within the Class. Silence doesn't bless something that was never eligible. So on Class Q, where there are so many factual ways to fall out — the gateway, the unit history, the caps, the works, the access — if any of that is genuinely arguable, the disciplined move is to get a certificate of lawfulness before you start work, because neither a prior approval nor the clock running out gives you any presumption that it's lawful. And a refusal, of course, carries the usual right of appeal.

Two conditions ride on the permission. You build it in accordance with the approved details — or, on deemed consent, the details you applied for. And you must complete it — finish it, not just start it — within three years. That completion point catches people, because unlike an ordinary permission, starting doesn't save you: a conversion that's still half-done at year three is carrying on without permission. Last thing — the space standard. The existing building has to be capable of delivering dwellings that meet the national space standard, and no unit can be a tiny box under thirty-seven square metres. Small buildings are simply out, and you can't extend your way in. So you design to the standard from the very start — which, in practice, also puts a ceiling on how many units you can realistically carve out, whatever floorspace the cap would otherwise allow.

title: Enforcement, Mansell and the fallback
paras: Finally, enforcement and the fallback — and one hard truth to open with. What's authorised is exactly what was described and approved, on the approved drawings. Build it differently, or do works beyond what's permitted, and you don't have a lawful conversion with a few defects — you've got development with no planning permission at all. Unlawful operations actually strip the change of use of its protection. And there's no tidying-up route afterwards — you can't use the usual amendment mechanisms on a prior approval. If the scheme changes after approval, you need a fresh prior approval, or a planning application for the bit that's changed, and you get that before you build it, not after.

A Class Q consent settles the planning position and absolutely nothing else — that's worth saying out loud to clients. You still need Building Regulations, and the structural, thermal, fire and drainage upgrades all have to be achievable within the limited works you're allowed — if they're not, you don't just fail building control, you fail Hibbitt, because it means the building couldn't really be converted. Barns are classic bat roosts and barn owl sites, so you need ecological survey in the right season, and possibly a protected species licence, whatever the permitted development right says. And the quiet killers: restrictive covenants, rights of way, drainage easements — private rights have sunk more than one fully consented conversion, so they belong on every due diligence list. The enforcement clock, by the way, is now ten years for recent breaches — so date any historic conversion carefully before you advise anyone on immunity.

Now the strategic side — the fallback — because this is where Class Q earns money even when you don't build it. There's a well-known case, Mansell, where a council granted permission for houses that conflicted with countryside policy, precisely because the realistic alternative was a Class Q conversion the officer thought would be a worse outcome. The Court of Appeal backed that. The principle is that a fallback is a material consideration wherever there's a real prospect of it happening — and that's a low bar, it doesn't have to be probable or certain — and how much weight it carries is for the decision-maker. With the new Class offering a fallback of up to ten dwellings rather than five, that's a genuinely powerful bargaining card.

But — and it's a big but — the fallback has to be real. An eligible building, the evidence actually assembled, ideally a prior approval already in hand, or at least a solid appraisal showing you'd get one. Inspectors and courts can smell a fallback that's been invented for the negotiation, and they'll give short shrift to a Class Q position that would collapse on Hibbitt, or on the unit history, or on one of the exclusions. And honestly, that's the theme of the whole topic. The mistakes people make are utterly predictable — reasoning from the old pre-2024 law, picking the wrong gateway, missing an intervening use or a Part 6 building, asserting a unit history instead of proving it, dressing a rebuild up as a conversion, relying on deemed consent when eligibility was shaky, then drifting off the approved drawings on site. Every one of them is avoidable with the same discipline: treat Class Q as a hard-edged eligibility exercise, and evidence it to the standard you'd need for a certificate.
